messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eleanor presents as a polished and articulate public servant, but her composure frays when she speaks of the fear that has governed her life for decades. Now thirty-nine, she is a respected City Council Member, a role she pursued to create the kind of safety and order she never knew as a child. The trauma dates back to her early childhood, a series of violent episodes she witnessed between her parents. She cannot construct a linear narrative of these events; her memory is a collection of searingly vivid snapshots separated by stretches of impenetrable fog. She can recall the exact pattern of the floral wallpaper in the hallway, the sound of a glass breaking against the kitchen wall, but the moments immediately following are a complete void, a silent, black space her mind refuses to enter. This fragmentation has been a constant, but in recent years, the snapshots have become more intrusive, more visceral.

The memories, when they surface, are not just mental images; they are full-body experiences. A sudden, loud noise in the street or a raised voice in a council meeting can trigger a fragment—the memory of her father’s heavy footsteps on the stairs, the acrid smell of his breath. In those moments, Eleanor finds her shoulders have hunched forward, her body instinctively trying to make itself smaller, a physical echo of the small child curled at the top of the stairs, listening. This somatic reenactment immediately plunges her into a state of high alert. The council chamber floor feels as unsteady as the worn linoleum of her childhood kitchen. Her focus shifts from the budget proposal to the faces in the room, scanning for a flicker of aggression, a tightening jaw, any sign that the contained anger of the debate might spill over into something physical. She has come to believe that danger is always imminent and that only her constant vigilance keeps it at bay.

This state of hypervigilance, in turn, acts as a magnet for the memories, creating a debilitating feedback loop. Standing at a public forum, listening to an angry constituent, Eleanor’s heart will begin to pound. This feeling of being a target, of being exposed to unchecked male anger, is enough to pull those same fragments to the surface. She won't just hear the constituent; she'll hear her father’s slurred shouting layered over it. She’ll see the man’s raised hand and, for a split second, it’s not a hand gesturing about zoning laws, but one about to strike. The present sense of threat summons the blueprint of all danger she has ever known, re-inscribing the terror and confirming her belief that she is never truly safe. The past and present collapse into one another, leaving her disoriented and terrified.

Over time, this cycle has dramatically constricted her life. Her world has shrunk to a few trusted locations. Her home, specifically her study, is the only place she feels a measure of peace. Public spaces, even her own city hall office, feel fraught with potential threats. She watches everyone, from colleagues to constituents, with a deep-seated suspicion, interpreting any abrupt movement or loud talk as a precursor to violence. This constant monitoring is exhausting and has taken a toll on her relationships and her work. She avoids after-hours functions and has delegated most of her public-facing duties, earning a reputation for being aloof. Sleep offers little respite; she lies awake for hours, her mind cataloging every creak of the house, unable to disarm the internal alarm system. Eleanor sought therapy after a particularly heated council debate last month, during which she was overwhelmed by a memory fragment so intense she had to feign illness and leave the room. She is terrified that this internal chaos will soon become visible, costing her the career she has built as her fortress against the past, and she is desperate to find a way to feel safe in her own life again.
